paragraphs.context: During the past year, many of my readers have requested that Jack and Annie visit the Titanic.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The writer explains why she wrote a book about the Titanic.
paragraphs.simple: Many children asked the writer to send Jack and Annie to the Titanic. At first she thought the story was too sad. But she listens carefully to children's ideas. She tried to find a way for Jack and Annie to help in this sad event. She talked with many children, and then she wrote the book. While she studied the real story, she learned how brave and calm people can be in a disaster. She thanks every child who asked for this book.
paragraphs.tone: Warm and thankful. The writer speaks to you like a friend.

background.note: The Titanic was a huge British passenger ship. It hit an iceberg and sank on its first trip, in April 1912. More than 1,500 people died. It is one of the most famous disasters in history.

paragraphs.context: One day in Frog Creek, Pennsylvania, a mysterious tree house appeared in the woods.
paragraphs.mainIdea: This part tells new readers the story of the series so far.
paragraphs.simple: Jack (8) and Annie (7) found a magic tree house full of books. If they point to a picture in a book and wish, the tree house takes them there. The tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay, a magic librarian. Jack and Annie helped Morgan, solved riddles, became Master Librarians and saved old stories. Now, in book 17, new adventures start.

background.note: Morgan le Fay is a magic woman from the old British stories about King Arthur. In this series she is kind and loves books.
King Arthur is a famous king in old British stories. He had brave knights who sat at a Round Table.
In books 9 to 12, Jack and Annie solved four riddles and became "Master Librarians": people who are very good at finding facts in books.

paragraphs.context: It was a stormy night. The rain tapped hard on his window pane.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A stormy night: the rain is hitting Jack's window.
paragraphs.simple: It is a night with wind and rain. The rain knocks hard on the glass of Jack's window, "tap, tap, tap".
paragraphs.tone: Dark and a little mysterious. A good start for an adventure.

paragraphs.context: The rain did seem to be tapping out Come now!
paragraphs.mainIdea: The sound of the rain seems to say "Come now!"
paragraphs.simple: Jack listens. The rain really does seem to tap the words "Come now! Come now!" like a message.
paragraphs.tone: Magic is starting. The writer uses the rain like a voice calling the children.

paragraphs.context: Jack didn’t want to leave his warm, cozy room.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wants to stay in bed, but he feels Annie is right.
paragraphs.simple: Jack likes his warm, comfortable room. He does not want to go out in the rain. But he feels something important will happen soon.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie went quietly down the stairs.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They leave the house quietly at night.
paragraphs.simple: They go down the stairs without noise, so their parents will not wake up. Then they go out into the cold, wet night.

background.note: "Slipped out the door" means went out quietly and quickly, so no one saw them.

paragraphs.context: The storm had eased up. Rain fell gently as they ran up the street.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The storm is weaker now, and they run to the woods.
paragraphs.simple: The storm is not so strong now. Light rain falls. The wet ground shines when the flashlight points at it.

paragraphs.context: Sitting in the corner was a small dog.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They find a small dog in the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: In the corner there is a little dog. He looks like a young terrier with messy, light brown hair.

background.note: A terrier is a kind of small, brave and lively dog. Many terriers have rough, untidy hair.

paragraphs.context: “He’s so cute,” she said. “He looks like a little teddy bear.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie names the dog Teddy.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks the dog looks like a soft toy bear, so she calls him "Teddy".

background.note: Teddy bears are named after the American president Theodore "Teddy" Roosevelt. In 1902 he would not shoot a bear on a hunting trip, and a toy maker made a soft toy bear called "Teddy's bear".

paragraphs.context: Jack’s gaze fell on a piece of paper lying on the floor.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack sees a note on the floor.
paragraphs.simple: Jack's eyes see a piece of paper on the floor. It is a note from Morgan.

paragraphs.context: This little dog is under a spell and needs your help.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan's note: the dog is under a magic spell.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan writes that a spell controls the little dog. To break the spell, Jack and Annie must be given four special gifts. Someone must give each gift to them; they cannot just take it.
paragraphs.tone: A riddle in a poem. Each gift is a clue for one adventure.

paragraphs.context: A gift from a ship lost at sea,
paragraphs.mainIdea: The first gift will come from a ship that sank.
paragraphs.simple: This line is part of Morgan's poem. The four lines tell where the four gifts will come from: a lost ship, the prairie, a faraway forest and a kangaroo (Australia).

paragraphs.context: A gift from the prairie blue,
paragraphs.mainIdea: The second gift will come from the prairie.
paragraphs.simple: The second gift will come from the wide, grassy land under a big blue sky.

background.note: "The prairie blue" means the prairie under a big blue sky. The writer puts the adjective after the noun to make the poem rhyme (blue / kangaroo). The next book (#18) goes to the American Great Plains.

paragraphs.context: P.S. Your Master Librarian cards won’t help on this mission.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan says their cards will not help this time.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan adds a short note: the Master Librarian cards will not help. Jack and Annie should just act like themselves, and things will be okay.

background.note: "P.S." means "postscript": something you add at the end of a letter, after your name.

paragraphs.context: The title of the book was The Unsinkable Ship.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Teddy chooses a book: The Unsinkable Ship.
paragraphs.simple: The dog pushes a book with his nose. The book is called The Unsinkable Ship: a ship that cannot sink.
paragraphs.tone: This is a sad joke for the reader. You know the Titanic DID sink, but Jack does not see it yet.

paragraphs.context: “Well, at least that’s good,” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks a ship that cannot sink is safe.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is happy: if the ship cannot sink, they will be safe, even if the ship is lost.
paragraphs.tone: Readers who know about the Titanic feel worried, because Jack is wrong.

paragraphs.context: Then everything was still.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house stops spinning.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house spins fast. Then it stops. Nothing moves.
paragraphs.tone: This is how every trip starts in the series. Short lines make it feel quiet and sudden.

paragraphs.context: “Wow, we’re dressed like old-fashioned kids!” she said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Their clothes have changed to old-style clothes.
paragraphs.simple: The magic gives them clothes from the time they visit. They are dressed like children from long ago.

paragraphs.context: Instead of pajamas and a poncho, she wore a sailor dress and a long wool cloak.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie's clothes from 1912.
paragraphs.simple: Annie now wears a sailor dress and a long, warm coat with no sleeves.

background.note: Sailor dresses and suits, with a big square collar, were very popular for children in the early 1900s.

paragraphs.context: Jack had on an overcoat and knee-length pants with long socks.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack's clothes from 1912.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wears a long coat, short pants that end at the knee, long socks, a shirt and a tie. Even his backpack is now made of leather.

background.note: In 1912, boys wore short pants until they were about 12 or 13. Long pants were for older boys and men.

paragraphs.context: The moonless sky glittered with stars.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A dark, clear night with many stars.
paragraphs.simple: There is no moon, but the sky is full of bright stars. The sea is calm.

background.note: On the night the Titanic sank there really was no moon, and the sea was very calm. This made the iceberg very hard to see.

paragraphs.context: The tree house seemed to be resting on a wooden deck between two giant columns.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house has landed on a ship.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house is sitting on the wooden floor of a ship, between two very tall round things. They are the ship's smokestacks.

background.note: The Titanic had four giant smokestacks (funnels). Only three let out smoke. The fourth was mostly for looks, to make the ship seem bigger and stronger.

paragraphs.context: “That must be the lookouts’ nest,” he said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack sees the high place where the lookouts watch.
paragraphs.simple: High on the front mast there is a small box. Sailors stood there and watched for danger.

background.note: It is usually called the "crow's nest". On the Titanic it was about 29 meters above the water. The lookouts had no binoculars that night.

paragraphs.context: Late at night, on April 14, 1912, an English ocean liner was making her first voyage across the Atlantic Ocean.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Facts from the book: the Titanic's first trip.
paragraphs.simple: On April 14, 1912, a big English ship was on its first trip across the Atlantic Ocean to New York. It carried 2,200 people and was very long. Most people thought it could not sink.

background.note: English often calls a ship "she" or "her". A ship's first trip is called its "maiden voyage". The Titanic left Southampton, England, on April 10, 1912.
The Titanic was about 269 meters long, nearly as long as three football fields.
The Atlantic Ocean is the big ocean between Europe and North America.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, man, we’re in 1912,” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack writes notes about the ship.
paragraphs.simple: Jack knows the year now. He writes in his notebook. (In the book, his notes are a picture, so the reader does not show the words.)

paragraphs.context: Just then, a shout came from the lookouts’ nest: “Iceberg ahead!”
paragraphs.mainIdea: The lookout sees an iceberg.
paragraphs.simple: Someone in the lookouts' nest shouts that there is an iceberg in front of the ship.

background.note: The real lookout was Frederick Fleet. He rang a bell three times and called "Iceberg, right ahead!" at about 11:40 at night. The ship turned, but it was too late.

paragraphs.context: The iceberg was dark with a fringe of white at the top.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The iceberg is right in front of the ship.
paragraphs.simple: The iceberg looks dark, with a thin line of white at the top. It is very close.

paragraphs.context: Jack felt a jolt. Then he heard a grinding sound.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ship hits the iceberg.
paragraphs.simple: Jack feels a sudden shake. He hears a rough, scraping sound: the side of the ship is rubbing against the ice.
paragraphs.tone: Short sentences make the moment feel sudden and scary.

paragraphs.context: “See?” Annie said to Teddy. “It was just a little bump.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie thinks the ship is fine.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks it was only a small knock. She believes the ship cannot sink. Jack is not so sure.

paragraphs.context: Without a word, she shined the flashlight on a life preserver hanging from the railing.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie shows Jack the ship's name.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says nothing. She points her light at a life ring on the railing. It has the ship's name on it.

paragraphs.context: R.M.S. TITANIC
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ship is the Titanic!
paragraphs.simple: Now they know: they are on the Titanic, and it has just hit an iceberg.
paragraphs.tone: The chapter ends with a shock. The reader knows what will happen.

background.note: R.M.S. means "Royal Mail Ship" (or Steamer). The Titanic carried letters (mail) for the British post office as well as people.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly, steam gushed out of the ship’s smokestacks.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ship's engines stop.
paragraphs.simple: Lots of steam rushes out of the smokestacks. The engines stop and the Titanic stops moving.

background.note: The Titanic's engines were steam engines. When the ship stopped, the extra steam had to be let out very loudly through the smokestacks.

paragraphs.context: “No! We have to stay and help,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie wants to stay and help.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they must stay. They can always leave in the tree house later.

paragraphs.context: “But what can we do?” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks they cannot change what happens.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says the ship will sink anyway. They cannot change the past, and they cannot take people home with them.
paragraphs.tone: Jack feels helpless. This is a big question in the book: how can you help when you cannot change history?

paragraphs.context: “Maybe they’re still asleep,” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Most people do not know about the danger yet.
paragraphs.simple: It is late at night. Most passengers are sleeping. They do not even know the ship hit an iceberg.

paragraphs.context: He saw exercise bikes and rowing machines in one room.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ship has a gym, a café and a library.
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees a room with exercise machines, a room with palm trees and bamboo chairs, and a library.

background.note: The Titanic had a gym with exercise bikes, rowing machines and even an "electric horse" for first-class passengers.

background.term: palm trees, bamboo chairs, and tables
background.note: This was the Titanic's "Café Parisien" and "Palm Court", where rich passengers sat among real palm plants.

paragraphs.context: “This ship is like a town,” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ship is so big that it is like a small town.
paragraphs.simple: The ship has so many rooms and things that Jack thinks it is like a whole town on the sea.

paragraphs.context: Jack heard a clicking noise as the man tapped a lever on a black box.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A man is sending a radio message.
paragraphs.simple: The man is using a radio machine. Each tap on the lever sends a short sound. That is how messages were sent in Morse code.

background.note: The radio operators on the Titanic were Jack Phillips and Harold Bride. They worked for the Marconi company and sent messages with a key that made clicks.

paragraphs.context: Another man stood nearby. He had a white beard and wore a fancy uniform.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The captain of the Titanic.
paragraphs.simple: A man with a white beard and a special uniform is there. He is the captain.

background.note: The Titanic's captain was Edward John Smith. He was 62 years old and planned to stop working after this trip. He went down with his ship.

paragraphs.context: “Send the international call for help,” he ordered the man with headphones.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The captain orders a call for help.
paragraphs.simple: The captain tells the radio man to send the call for help that all countries know. All ships near them must come quickly, because the ship is sinking.

paragraphs.context: After the Titanic hit the iceberg at 11:40 P.M., the ship’s radio operator sent out an SOS.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Facts from the book: the SOS message.
paragraphs.simple: The Titanic hit the iceberg at 11:40 at night. The radio man sent "SOS", the call for help. The nearest ship had turned its radio off. Other ships got the message but were too far away. The Titanic sank at about 2:20 in the morning, all alone.

background.note: SOS is a call for help in Morse code: three short, three long, three short sounds (... --- ...). The Titanic was one of the first ships ever to send SOS.

background.term: the only ship near the Titanic
background.note: This ship was the Californian. It was only about 20 to 30 km away, but its radio man had gone to bed.
P.M. means after noon (afternoon or night). A.M. means before noon (night or morning).

paragraphs.context: “Tell the men to start loading the lifeboats now,” the captain ordered a deck hand.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The captain orders the lifeboats to be filled.
paragraphs.simple: The captain tells a sailor to start putting people into the lifeboats.

paragraphs.context: On the Titanic, there were 20 lifeboats.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Facts from the book: not enough lifeboats.
paragraphs.simple: There were only 20 lifeboats. The ship needed two times more. In the confusion, some boats left half empty. Many poor passengers on the lower decks did not know where to go.

background.note: The 20 lifeboats had seats for about 1,178 people, but there were about 2,200 people on board. The law in 1912 did not ask for more.
Third class was the cheapest ticket. Many third-class passengers were families moving to America to start a new life.

paragraphs.context: “Hey, I know what we can do to help,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie has an idea.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they can help people find the lifeboats. Jack agrees: their book has a map of the ship.

paragraphs.context: “We’ll start at the grand stairway,” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They make a plan with the map.
paragraphs.simple: Jack moves his finger along the map. They will start at the big beautiful stairs and go down to the cheap rooms.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked back through the door.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The radio man keeps sending SOS.
paragraphs.simple: The radio man is still sending his message, again and again.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie slipped through a door off the boat deck.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They go inside the ship.
paragraphs.simple: They go quickly and quietly through a door from the deck with the lifeboats. Teddy follows close behind them.

background.note: The boat deck was the top open deck of the Titanic, where the lifeboats were kept.

paragraphs.context: They were at the top of the empty grand stairway.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The beautiful Grand Staircase.
paragraphs.simple: The stairs are made of dark, shiny wood. Above them there is a big round glass roof with lights.

background.note: The Titanic's Grand Staircase was famous for its beauty. It had carved wood, a large glass dome and a big clock. It was for first-class passengers.

paragraphs.context: The hands of the clock were at 12:20.
paragraphs.mainIdea: It is 12:20 at night.
paragraphs.simple: The clock shows twenty minutes after midnight. Jack knows the ship will sink at 2:20, so there are only two hours left.

paragraphs.context: “Hey, look,” said Annie. “The floor’s slanting down.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: The floor is not flat any more.
paragraphs.simple: Annie sees that the floor goes down at one end. Jack understands: the front of the ship is going under the water.

paragraphs.context: Men and women stumbled out of their rooms.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Rich passengers come out of their rooms.
paragraphs.simple: Sleepy people come out of their rooms. They wear beautiful, expensive night robes.

background.note: Velvet was an expensive, soft cloth. The writer shows that these are rich first-class passengers.

paragraphs.context: “There’s been a little accident,” the man in the uniform said cheerfully.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The worker does not tell the truth about the danger.
paragraphs.simple: The man says it is only a small accident, in a happy voice. He does not want people to panic.
paragraphs.tone: The happy voice is sad for the reader, because we know how bad it is.

paragraphs.context: These people were not dressed in fancy clothes.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Third-class passengers are not worried either.
paragraphs.simple: These poorer people wear simple dark coats. They are not worried. They are joking and laughing.

paragraphs.context: Four men were playing cards.
paragraphs.mainIdea: People are still having fun.
paragraphs.simple: In a smoky room, men play cards, a woman plays the piano, and a young man and woman dance.
paragraphs.tone: Everything seems normal and happy. This makes the danger feel even worse.

paragraphs.context: The floor was really slanting down here, and water sloshed at the end of a hallway.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Water is coming into the ship.
paragraphs.simple: Down here the floor slopes a lot. At the end of the hall, water moves and splashes.

paragraphs.context: Teddy whined. Jack buried his face in the little dog’s fur.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack feels very sad.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy makes a sad sound. Jack pushes his face into the dog's soft fur, because he feels so sad.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly, the dog leaped out of Jack’s arms. He charged down the hall.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Teddy runs toward the water.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy jumps out of Jack's arms and runs fast down the hall, straight toward the water.

paragraphs.context: The boy wore a nightshirt. He had red hair and freckles.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They meet a little boy.
paragraphs.simple: A small boy in night clothes opens the door. He has red hair and brown spots on his face. He is about four years old.

paragraphs.context: “Hello,” she said. She put her arm around the little boy.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They meet Lucy and William.
paragraphs.simple: The girl is Lucy O'Malley. The little boy is her brother, William.

background.note: O'Malley is an Irish family name. Many third-class passengers on the Titanic came from Ireland. The ship stopped in Queenstown, Ireland, to pick them up.

paragraphs.context: “Our parents aren’t here. They’re in New York,” she said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children are traveling alone.
paragraphs.simple: Lucy and William's parents are already in New York. The children are going to meet them there.

background.note: Many people moved from Europe to America at this time. Often parents went first to find work, and the children came later.

paragraphs.context: Jack didn’t feel any extra weight in his knapsack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Teddy weighs nothing.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy is in the knapsack, but Jack cannot feel any weight. The dog seems to weigh as little as air.
paragraphs.tone: A small clue that Teddy is magic.

paragraphs.context: When Lucy came out, Jack saw her slip something into her coat pocket.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lucy takes something secret.
paragraphs.simple: Lucy quickly puts something in her pocket. We find out later: it is her father's watch.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly, he felt freezing water brush against his shoes.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The cold water reaches them.
paragraphs.simple: Very cold sea water touches Jack's shoes. The water is coming down the hall.

background.note: The water that night was about −2 °C. Salt water can be colder than 0 °C without turning to ice. People in the water could only live for a few minutes.

paragraphs.context: The water was creeping up the stairs, step by step.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The water is climbing the stairs.
paragraphs.simple: The water moves slowly up the stairs, one step after another.

paragraphs.context: “Little girl,” one said with a laugh,
paragraphs.mainIdea: The card players do not believe Annie.
paragraphs.simple: A man laughs. He says even if the ship sinks, it will be slow, and everyone will be saved.

paragraphs.context: “Indeed. Many ships are on their way right now,” another man said in a soothing voice.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The men think help is coming.
paragraphs.simple: Another man says calmly that many ships are coming to help. He thinks there is nothing to worry about.
paragraphs.tone: The men are calm because they do not understand the danger.

paragraphs.context: On the top deck, the Titanic was as bright as a Christmas tree.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The top deck is full of lights and music.
paragraphs.simple: The ship's lights are all on, so it shines like a Christmas tree.

background.term: as bright as a Christmas tree
background.note: The ship's engineers stayed at work deep inside the ship, so the lights stayed on until the very end. None of the engineers lived.

paragraphs.context: A band played lively music.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The band plays happy music.
paragraphs.simple: Musicians play fast, happy music to keep people calm.

background.note: The Titanic's eight musicians, led by Wallace Hartley, played on deck to keep people calm. None of them lived.

paragraphs.context: With a hiss and rush of light, a rocket streaked into the sky.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A rocket goes up into the sky.
paragraphs.simple: A rocket shoots up with a hissing sound and explodes into colored lights.

background.note: These were distress rockets. The Titanic fired eight rockets to ask other ships for help. The Californian saw them, but did not understand.

paragraphs.context: “This is a trick, isn’t it?” she said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lucy thinks it is a party.
paragraphs.simple: Lucy thinks Jack and Annie have tricked them. With music and fireworks, it looks like a party.

paragraphs.context: “Women and children first!” someone shouted.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Women and children go into the lifeboats first.
paragraphs.simple: Someone shouts the old sea rule: women and children get into the lifeboats before men.

background.note: On the Titanic, the officers followed this rule. About 74% of the women and 52% of the children lived, but only about 20% of the men.

paragraphs.context: The lifeboat was waiting to go down.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The small lifeboat hangs at the side of the ship.
paragraphs.simple: The lifeboat hangs on ropes at the side of the big ship. It looks very small. The sea below is black.

paragraphs.context: Jack understood. The brightly lit Titanic seemed so solid and safe compared to the little lifeboat.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The big ship seems safer than the little boat.
paragraphs.simple: Jack understands why Lucy is afraid. The big ship, full of lights, seems strong and safe. The little boat does not.

background.note: This is why many of the first lifeboats left half empty. Many people did not want to leave the big, bright, warm ship.

paragraphs.context: “You have to be brave now,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie tells Lucy to be brave for William.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says Lucy must be brave, to help her little brother.

paragraphs.context: She reached into her coat pocket and pulled out a silver watch on a chain.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lucy gives them a gift.
paragraphs.simple: Lucy takes out a silver pocket watch. It is her father's. She gives it to Jack and Annie.

background.note: In 1912 many men carried a "pocket watch" on a chain instead of wearing a watch on the wrist.

paragraphs.context: “This is a gift for both of you,” she said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is the first gift for Teddy.
paragraphs.simple: Lucy says the watch brought them good luck. She feels Jack and Annie were their good luck tonight.
paragraphs.tone: A happy and sad moment. This is the "gift from a ship lost at sea" in Morgan's poem.

paragraphs.context: “Into the lifeboat, my dear!” the man said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A man puts Annie into the lifeboat.
paragraphs.simple: The man thinks Annie is a passenger, so he throws her into the lifeboat. Jack jumps away so the man cannot take him.

paragraphs.context: The lifeboat jerked. It started creaking down toward the dark, cold sea.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The lifeboat goes down with Annie in it.
paragraphs.simple: The lifeboat moves suddenly. It goes down toward the sea, with noisy ropes and wood.

paragraphs.context: “Bring the boat back up for Lady Blackwell!”
paragraphs.mainIdea: The lifeboat is brought back up for a rich woman.
paragraphs.simple: A woman in an expensive fur coat wants to get into the lifeboat. The man stops the boat and brings it back up for her.

background.note: "Lady" before a name is a title for a woman from an important British family. Many very rich people were on the Titanic.

paragraphs.context: Jack pushed his way forward.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack pulls Annie back onto the ship.
paragraphs.simple: The lifeboat comes back up to the level of the deck. Jack reaches out, and Annie grabs his hands. He pulls her back.

paragraphs.context: They saw Lucy and William’s little lifeboat creaking down toward the Atlantic Ocean.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lucy and William's boat goes away safely.
paragraphs.simple: The little boat goes down to the smooth, black water. Then it floats away into the dark.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly, the front of the ship dipped down into the sea.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The front of the ship goes under the water.
paragraphs.simple: The front of the ship goes down into the sea. Deck chairs begin to slide.

paragraphs.context: The band played a slow, calm song. It sounded like a church hymn.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The band plays a slow church song.
paragraphs.simple: Now the music is slow and calm, like a song in church.

background.note: Many survivors said the band's last song was the hymn "Nearer, My God, to Thee". No one knows for sure.

paragraphs.context: “It’s every man for himself!” the captain shouted to all of his crew.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The captain tells his crew to save themselves.
paragraphs.simple: The captain says each man must now save himself. The workers stop their jobs and run.

background.note: Some survivors said Captain Smith told his crew this near the end. It means "Your work is done; try to save yourselves".

paragraphs.context: The magic tree house was gone!
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house is not there!
paragraphs.simple: They reach the smokestacks, but they cannot see the tree house.
paragraphs.tone: A scary end to the chapter. How will they get home?

paragraphs.context: Jack imagined everything crashing forward—all the furniture, dishes, bicycles, the grand clock on the staircase.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack imagines everything inside the ship falling.
paragraphs.simple: Jack pictures all the things inside the ship sliding forward and breaking.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly, the lights on the Titanic went out.
paragraphs.mainIdea: All the lights go out.
paragraphs.simple: The lights stop. Everything is totally dark.

background.note: The Titanic's lights went out at about 2:18 A.M., a minute or two before it sank.

paragraphs.context: The back of the Titanic was rising out of the ocean.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The back of the ship goes up.
paragraphs.simple: The front of the ship goes down, so the back lifts high out of the water.

background.note: As the back of the ship rose, the Titanic broke into two pieces. People did not know this for sure until the wreck was found in 1985.

paragraphs.context: In the dark, he could barely see the tree house.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack finds the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: Jack can only just see the tree house. It is stuck between a smokestack and the railing, lying on its side.

paragraphs.context: Jack heard a loud CRA-A-A-ACK!
paragraphs.mainIdea: A loud breaking sound.
paragraphs.simple: Jack hears a very loud crack as they leave. It is the sound of the ship breaking.
paragraphs.tone: The long "CRA-A-A-ACK" shows a huge, slow, terrible sound.

paragraphs.context: He thought of the Titanic sinking into the cold black sea.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack cries for the Titanic.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks about the ship going down in the cold sea. Tears come into his eyes.

paragraphs.context: “I think he has a touch of magic,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Teddy has some magic.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks Teddy has a little magic, because he got out of the knapsack by himself.

paragraphs.context: The watch had stopped. The hands were at 2:20.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The watch stopped at 2:20.
paragraphs.simple: The watch stopped at 2:20, the exact time the Titanic sank.

background.note: The Titanic sank at about 2:20 A.M. on April 15, 1912, two hours and forty minutes after it hit the iceberg.

paragraphs.context: “He’s up to his magic tricks again,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Teddy has disappeared.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says Teddy is doing his magic again. "Be up to something" means doing something secret or clever. They must go home without him.

paragraphs.context: “Time might have stopped for the Titanic,” Jack said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Books and memories keep the Titanic alive.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says the Titanic is gone, but people still remember it through books. It is a true story, but now it is told like an old story.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah,” said Annie. “And every time the story’s told, we wish it had a different ending.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: We always wish the story ended differently.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says that each time people tell the story, they wish the ship did not sink.

paragraphs.context: Then he and Annie slipped quietly into their house,
paragraphs.mainIdea: They are home and safe.
paragraphs.simple: They go quietly into their warm, dry, safe house.
paragraphs.tone: A calm, safe ending after a scary night.

paragraphs.context: 1) The Titanic hit the iceberg in the North Atlantic,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Where the Titanic sank.
paragraphs.simple: The Titanic hit the iceberg in the north of the Atlantic Ocean, about 400 miles (about 640 km) from Newfoundland.

background.note: Newfoundland is a large island on the east coast of Canada.

paragraphs.context: 2) The Titanic was considered unsinkable
paragraphs.mainIdea: Why people thought it could not sink, and why it did.
paragraphs.simple: The ship had strong doors inside to stop water. But the iceberg opened six of the closed rooms at the bottom, so water filled them and the ship sank.

background.note: The Titanic could stay up with four compartments full of water, but not with five or six.

paragraphs.context: 5) More than 1,500 people perished in the Titanic disaster,
paragraphs.mainIdea: How many people died and lived.
paragraphs.simple: More than 1,500 people died. 705 people got away in lifeboats. The ship Carpathia picked them up.

background.note: The Carpathia was about 93 km away. It came as fast as it could and arrived at about 4 A.M., after the Titanic had sunk.

paragraphs.context: 6) After the sinking of the Titanic, laws were changed
paragraphs.mainIdea: New rules after the Titanic.
paragraphs.simple: After the Titanic, ships had to carry enough lifeboats for everyone. A group was formed to warn ships about ice.

background.note: The International Ice Patrol started in 1914. Today it still watches for icebergs in the North Atlantic, using planes and satellites.

paragraphs.context: 7) In 1985, a scientist named Dr. Robert Ballard discovered the undersea wreck of the Titanic.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The wreck was found in 1985.
paragraphs.simple: In 1985, a scientist found what is left of the Titanic at the bottom of the sea.

background.note: Robert Ballard is an American ocean scientist. He found the wreck about 3,800 meters under the sea, in two big pieces.

sentences.context: However, as more and more requests came in, I began to think about it, for I take the suggestions of kids very seriously.
sentences.simple: But more and more children asked. So I started to think about it, because I think children's ideas are important.
sentences.main: I began to think about it.

parts.meaning: But.

parts.text: as more and more requests came in,
parts.meaning: while I got more and more letters asking for it,

parts.text: I began to think about it,
parts.meaning: I started to think about the idea,

parts.text: for I take the suggestions of kids very seriously.
parts.meaning: because I think children's ideas are important.

sentences.grammar: "For" here means "because". This is an old, written use. "More and more" means the number keeps growing.

sentences.context: So I tried to think of a way that Jack and Annie might actually be helpful in the midst of such a tragedy.
sentences.simple: So I tried to find a way for Jack and Annie to really help, in the middle of this very sad event.
sentences.main: I tried to think of a way.

parts.text: So I tried to think of a way
parts.meaning: So I tried to find a way

parts.text: that Jack and Annie might actually be helpful
parts.meaning: for Jack and Annie to really help

parts.text: in the midst of such a tragedy.
parts.meaning: in the middle of such a sad event.

sentences.grammar: "That ..." tells you about "a way". "Might" means maybe. "Such a" + noun makes it stronger: "such a tragedy" = a very sad event like this.

sentences.context: While researching the true story of the Titanic, I learned a lot about human dignity and courage in the face of disaster.
sentences.simple: When I studied the true story, I learned that people can be calm, proud and brave in a terrible event.
sentences.main: I learned a lot.

parts.text: While researching the true story of the Titanic,
parts.meaning: When I was studying the real story of the Titanic,
I learned many things
about how calm and brave people can be
when something terrible happens.

sentences.grammar: "While + -ing" means "when I was doing". The person (I) is the same in both parts, so the writer does not say "I" again after "While".

sentences.context: Morgan is a magical librarian from the time of King Arthur. She travels through time and space, gathering books.
sentences.simple: Morgan is a magic librarian from King Arthur's time. She goes to different times and places to collect books.
sentences.main: She travels through time and space.

parts.text: Morgan is a magical librarian from the time of King Arthur.
parts.meaning: Morgan is a magic librarian from King Arthur's time.

parts.text: She travels through time and space,
parts.meaning: She goes to many times and places,

parts.job: What she does at the same time.
parts.meaning: and collects books.

sentences.grammar: The "-ing" part ("gathering books") tells you what she does while she travels.

sentences.context: They headed into the Frog Creek woods. Wind blew through the trees, shaking water to the ground.
sentences.simple: They went into the woods. The wind blew the trees, and water fell down from them.
sentences.main: Wind blew through the trees.

parts.text: They headed into the Frog Creek woods.
parts.meaning: They went into the Frog Creek woods.
The wind moved through the trees,
and it shook the water off the leaves onto the ground.

sentences.grammar: "Headed" means "went toward". The "-ing" part ("shaking water ...") tells you what the wind did at the same time.

sentences.context: This little dog is under a spell and needs your help. To free him, you must be given four special things:
sentences.simple: Magic controls this dog, and he needs help. To make him free, someone must give you four special things.
sentences.main: This little dog needs your help.

parts.text: This little dog is under a spell
parts.meaning: Magic is controlling this little dog
and he needs you to help him.
To make him free from the magic,

parts.text: you must be given four special things:
parts.meaning: other people must give you four special things:

sentences.grammar: "Must be given" is a passive verb: someone must give the things TO you. So you cannot just find or take them.

sentences.context: The tree house seemed to be resting on a wooden deck between two giant columns.
sentences.simple: The tree house looked like it was sitting on a wooden floor between two very tall round posts.
sentences.main: The tree house seemed to be resting.

parts.text: The tree house seemed to be resting
parts.meaning: The tree house looked like it was sitting
on a wooden ship floor
between two very tall round things.

sentences.grammar: "Seem to be + -ing" means "looks like it is doing". Jack cannot see well in the dark, so he is not sure.

sentences.context: Late at night, on April 14, 1912, an English ocean liner was making her first voyage across the Atlantic Ocean.
sentences.simple: Late on the night of April 14, 1912, a big English passenger ship was on its first trip across the Atlantic Ocean.
sentences.main: An English ocean liner was making her first voyage.

parts.meaning: Late at night on April 14, 1912,

parts.text: an English ocean liner was making her first voyage
parts.meaning: a big English passenger ship was on its first trip
over the Atlantic Ocean.

sentences.grammar: "Was making" (past continuous) shows something that was going on at that time. The ship is "her": English often calls ships "she".

sentences.context: Carrying 2,200 passengers, the ship was four city blocks long.
sentences.simple: The ship had 2,200 people on it, and it was as long as four city streets.
sentences.main: The ship was four city blocks long.

parts.meaning: It had 2,200 passengers on it.

parts.text: the ship was four city blocks long.
parts.meaning: The ship was very long, as long as four city blocks.

sentences.grammar: The "-ing" part at the start ("Carrying ...") tells you more about the ship. "Number + noun + long" gives length: "four city blocks long".

sentences.context: Jack and Annie turned back to the window—just in time to see a huge iceberg looming out of the sea.
sentences.simple: Jack and Annie looked out of the window again. They were just in time to see a huge iceberg appear out of the dark sea.
sentences.main: Jack and Annie turned back to the window.

parts.text: Jack and Annie turned back to the window
parts.meaning: Jack and Annie looked out of the window again

parts.text: —just in time to see a huge iceberg
parts.meaning: and right at that moment they saw a huge iceberg
coming up out of the sea, big and dark.

sentences.grammar: "See + thing + -ing" means you see something while it is happening: "see a huge iceberg looming".

sentences.context: The scraping sound stopped. The ship slid past the iceberg until they lost sight of it.
sentences.simple: The scraping noise stopped. The ship moved past the iceberg, and then they could not see it any more.
sentences.main: The ship slid past the iceberg.

parts.meaning: The rough noise stopped.

parts.text: The ship slid past the iceberg
parts.meaning: The ship moved smoothly past the iceberg

parts.text: until they lost sight of it.
parts.meaning: until they could not see it any more.

sentences.grammar: "Slid" is the past of "slide". "Lose sight of" = not see any more.

sentences.context: “This ship’s going to sink no matter what. We can’t change history.
sentences.simple: This ship will sink in any case. We cannot change what happened in the past.
sentences.main: This ship is going to sink.

parts.meaning: This ship is going to sink
whatever we do.
We cannot change the past.

sentences.grammar: "Ship's" here is "ship is". "Be going to" talks about something sure to happen in the future.

sentences.context: Unfortunately, the only ship near the Titanic had turned off its radio for the night.
sentences.simple: Sadly, the one ship that was close to the Titanic had switched off its radio for the night.
sentences.main: The only ship had turned off its radio.

parts.meaning: Sadly,

parts.text: the only ship near the Titanic
parts.meaning: the one ship that was close to the Titanic
had already switched off its radio
until the morning.

sentences.grammar: "Had turned off" is the past perfect. It happened BEFORE the SOS was sent, so no one heard it.

sentences.context: All the other ships who received the message were too far away to help.
sentences.simple: The other ships got the message, but they were too far away to help.
sentences.main: All the other ships were too far away.

parts.meaning: All the other ships
that got the SOS message

parts.text: were too far away to help.
parts.meaning: could not help, because they were too far away.

sentences.grammar: "Too + adjective + to do" means "so ... that you cannot do it". Here "too far away to help" = so far away that they could not help.

sentences.context: But with all the confusion on board, a number of the lifeboats were not even full when they left the ship.
sentences.simple: But people on the ship were confused, so some lifeboats were not full when they went away.
sentences.main: A number of the lifeboats were not even full.

parts.text: But with all the confusion on board,
parts.meaning: But because everyone on the ship was confused,

parts.text: a number of the lifeboats were not even full
parts.meaning: some of the lifeboats were not full
when they went away from the ship.

sentences.grammar: "A number of" means "some" or "several". "Not even" makes it stronger: you would expect them to be full, but they were not.

sentences.context: Many third-class passengers did not have a chance to get into any of the lifeboats because they were on the lower decks and didn’t know where to go.
sentences.simple: Many poor passengers could not get into the lifeboats. They were on the low floors and did not know the way.
sentences.main: Many third-class passengers did not have a chance.

parts.meaning: Many people with the cheapest tickets

parts.text: did not have a chance to get into any of the lifeboats
parts.meaning: could not get into any lifeboat

parts.text: because they were on the lower decks
parts.meaning: because they were on the lower floors of the ship

parts.text: and didn’t know where to go.
parts.meaning: and did not know the way.

sentences.grammar: "Have a chance to do" = be able to do. "Where to go" = which way they should go.

sentences.context: The floor was really slanting down here, and water sloshed at the end of a hallway.
sentences.simple: Down here the floor sloped a lot, and water splashed around at the end of a hall.
sentences.main: The floor was really slanting down here.

parts.text: The floor was really slanting down here,
parts.meaning: Here the floor went down a lot,

parts.text: and water sloshed at the end of a hallway.
parts.meaning: and water moved and splashed at the end of a hall.

sentences.grammar: Two short sentences joined with "and". "Was slanting" (past continuous) shows it was happening at that time.

sentences.context: “Little girl,” one said with a laugh, “even if this ship does sink, it will take all night.
sentences.simple: One man laughed and said, "Little girl, if this ship really sinks, it will be very slow."
sentences.main: It will take all night.

parts.text: “Little girl,” one said with a laugh,
parts.meaning: One man laughed and said: "Little girl,
if this ship really sinks,
it will need the whole night."

sentences.grammar: "Does sink" uses "does" to make the verb stronger: "really sinks". "It takes + time" = you need that much time.

sentences.context: There’s plenty of time for everyone on board to be rescued.”
sentences.simple: There is a lot of time, so everyone on the ship can be saved.
sentences.main: There's plenty of time.

parts.meaning: There is a lot of time
for all the people on the ship
to be saved.

sentences.grammar: "To be rescued" is passive: other people will rescue them. "For + person + to do" = so that the person can do it.

sentences.context: The brightly lit Titanic seemed so solid and safe compared to the little lifeboat.
sentences.simple: The Titanic, full of bright lights, looked very strong and safe next to the small lifeboat.
sentences.main: The Titanic seemed so solid and safe.

parts.meaning: The Titanic, full of bright lights,
looked very strong and safe
when you looked at it next to the small lifeboat.

sentences.grammar: "Lit" is the past form of "light" and here means "with the lights on". "Compared to" + noun: when you think about the two things together.

sentences.context: I have a feeling that the two of you were our good luck tonight.”
sentences.simple: I think you two brought us good luck tonight.
sentences.main: I have a feeling.

parts.meaning: I think (but I am not sure)

parts.text: that the two of you were our good luck tonight.”
parts.meaning: that you two were what brought us good luck tonight.

sentences.grammar: "Have a feeling that ..." is a soft way to say "I think".

sentences.context: But the crowd started to panic. People pushed and shouted, trying to get to a safer part of the ship.
sentences.simple: But the people became very afraid. They pushed and shouted. They tried to get to a safer place on the ship.
sentences.main: The crowd started to panic.

parts.text: But the crowd started to panic.
parts.meaning: But the people became so afraid they could not think clearly.
People pushed and shouted,

parts.text: trying to get to a safer part of the ship.
parts.meaning: because they wanted to get to a safer place on the ship.

sentences.grammar: "Trying to ..." (an -ing part) explains what they wanted at the same time.

sentences.context: Jack imagined everything crashing forward—all the furniture, dishes, bicycles, the grand clock on the staircase.
sentences.simple: Jack pictured everything falling forward: the furniture, dishes, bikes and the big clock on the stairs.
sentences.main: Jack imagined everything crashing forward.

parts.meaning: Jack pictured everything falling forward and breaking

parts.text: —all the furniture, dishes, bicycles, the grand clock on the staircase.
parts.meaning: the furniture, the dishes, the bikes, and the big clock on the stairs.

sentences.grammar: "Imagine + thing + -ing" means you see it in your mind as it happens. The dash (—) starts a list of examples.

sentences.context: In the dark, he could barely see the tree house. It was stuck between a smokestack and the railing.
sentences.simple: In the dark, Jack could only just see the tree house. It was caught between a smokestack and the railing.
sentences.main: He could barely see the tree house.

parts.meaning: Because it was dark,

parts.text: he could barely see the tree house.
parts.meaning: he could almost not see the tree house.

parts.text: It was stuck between a smokestack and the railing.
parts.meaning: It was caught between a smokestack and the railing and could not move.

sentences.grammar: "Barely" means "only just; almost not". "Stuck" is the past form of "stick": here it means caught and not able to move.

sentences.context: “But books and memories keep the Titanic alive, don’t they?
sentences.simple: But because of books and memories, the Titanic is still with us, isn't it?
sentences.main: Books and memories keep the Titanic alive.

parts.meaning: But books and the things people remember
make the Titanic live on,
right?

sentences.grammar: "Keep + thing + adjective" means make something stay that way: "keep the Titanic alive". "Don't they?" at the end is a question tag that asks the listener to agree.

sentences.context: “And every time the story’s told, we wish it had a different ending.”
sentences.simple: Every time people tell the story, we wish it ended in a different way.
sentences.main: We wish it had a different ending.

parts.meaning: And each time someone tells the story,

parts.text: we wish it had a different ending.”
parts.meaning: we wish it ended in another way.

sentences.grammar: "Story's told" = "story is told" (passive). "Wish + past tense" talks about something that is not true: the ending is sad, and we wish it were not.

sentences.context: Staring at the starry sky, he shuddered at the memory of the sinking ship.
sentences.simple: Jack looked for a long time at the sky full of stars. He shook when he remembered the ship going down.
sentences.main: He shuddered at the memory.

parts.meaning: While he looked at the sky full of stars,
he shook with fear

parts.text: at the memory of the sinking ship.
parts.meaning: when he remembered the ship going down.

sentences.grammar: The "-ing" part at the start ("Staring at ...") tells you what Jack was doing at the same time.

sentences.context: However, when the ship hit the iceberg, six watertight compartments quickly filled up with water, dooming the ship.
sentences.simple: But when the ship hit the iceberg, six closed rooms at the bottom filled with water very fast. Because of this, the ship had to sink.
sentences.main: Six watertight compartments filled up with water.

parts.meaning: But

parts.text: when the ship hit the iceberg,
parts.meaning: when the ship hit the iceberg,

parts.text: six watertight compartments quickly filled up with water,
parts.meaning: six closed spaces at the bottom quickly filled with water,
and so the ship was sure to sink.

sentences.grammar: The "-ing" part at the end ("dooming the ship") shows the result of the main part.
